Wadgassen
VAHD-gah-sun
n. (the Saarland Premonstratensian abbey of 1135, whose site became a glassworks)
From Old High German, the dwelling at the ford; wad, a ford, and gassen, lanes.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Wadgassen on the Saar was founded in 1135 by Count Frederick of Saarbrücken and given to the Premonstratensians, and it held lands on both banks of a river that would become one of Europe's most contested borders. It was destroyed by French troops in 1793 and finally dissolved in 1795. In 1843 Villeroy & Boch bought the site and built a glassworks on it, which ran until 1995; the abbey's library, remarkably, survived and is now a museum of printing. This dictionary records Wadgassen for the glass, because Scripture uses glass for one purpose above all others, and it is not decoration. We see indirectly now, “For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face” (1Co 13:12), and the knowing is correspondingly partial, “now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known” (1Co 13:12). The same figure is used of a man who forgets what he looked like, “he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass” (Jam 1:23), and the glass that does change a man is the one that shows him Christ, “But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image” (2Co 3:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines glass as a hard brittle transparent substance; a mirror as a looking glass; transparent as admitting light so objects can be seen through; to reflect as to throw back rays; and darkly as obscurely.

expand to see more

GLASS, n. A hard, brittle, transparent, factitious substance, formed by fusing sand with fixed alkalies; also, a looking glass; a mirror.

MIRROR, n. A looking glass; any glass or polished substance that forms images by the reflection of rays of light.

TRANSPARENT, adj. Having the property of transmitting rays of light, so that bodies can be distinctly seen through; pervious to light.

REFLECT, v.t. To throw back; as, a mirror reflects the rays of light; to cast back the image of.

DARKLY, adv. Obscurely; dimly; blindly; uncertainly; with imperfect light, clearness or knowledge.

Key Scripture

1Co 13:12 — "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known."

Jam 1:23 — "For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass:"

2Co 3:18 — "But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord."

Col 2:3 — "In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge."

Modern Corruption

Saarland Premonstratensian abbey of 1135: destroyed in the Revolution, rebuilt as a glassworks, and its library survives as a museum of printing.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Paul's honesty about how much we currently see. The mirrors of the ancient world were polished metal and gave a dim, warped image, which is exactly the force of the figure, “For now we see through a glass, darkly” (1Co 13:12). He applies it to knowledge without flinching, “now I know in part” (1Co 13:12), which is a useful corrective to anyone certain he has the whole picture.

The second use of the figure is moral. James describes a man who looks in a glass and walks away having forgotten his own face, which is his picture of hearing without doing, “he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass” (Jam 1:23). Against that, Paul describes a looking that actually transforms the looker, “are changed into the same image from glory to glory” (2Co 3:18). The treasures a man is actually looking for are located in one place, “In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col 2:3).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek esoptron (G2072), a mirror; Greek ainigma (G135), an enigma; Greek katoptrizomai (G2734), to behold as in a glass; Greek metamorphoo (G3339), to transform; Greek apokruphos (G614), hidden.

expand to see more

Greek esoptron (G2072) — a mirror of polished metal; “For now we see through a glass, darkly”, 1 Corinthians 13:12.

Greek meros (G3313) — a part, the measure of present knowledge; “now I know in part”, 1 Corinthians 13:12.

Greek katanoeo (G2657) — to observe carefully, then forget; “beholding his natural face in a glass”, James 1:23.

Greek metamorphoo (G3339) — to be transformed by looking; “are changed into the same image”, 2 Corinthians 3:18.

Greek thesauros (G2344) — a treasure, hidden in Christ; “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge”, Colossians 2:3.

Usage

"“For now we see through a glass, darkly” (1Co 13:12) — a warped metal mirror, not a window."

"“beholding his natural face in a glass” (Jam 1:23) — hearing without doing."

"“are changed into the same image from glory to glory” (2Co 3:18) — the looking that alters the looker."
